FOR YOU

Based on one randomised trial, vision screening alone may make no difference to near vision compared with not screening. The evidence for this is low certainty, so we are not sure of the result.

Claim: Near visual acuity may show no difference between vision screening alone and no vision screening (low-certainty evidence).

[source: pmid:18614568]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Here is what the review of the research found about your depression medicine.

Claim: Based on moderate-certainty evidence, there is probably no difference in improvement in depression symptoms between SSRIs and placebo.

In plain terms: the studies suggest SSRI medicines probably do not help depression symptoms more than a placebo (a sugar pill). The evidence is moderately strong but not certain. The two studies included in this review involved people with COPD, a lung condition, so they may not match your own situation. Your clinician will look at your full health history and decide together with you what is right for you. Please talk with them before you change or stop any medicine.

[source: pmid:25308771; pmid:17136950]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: This note is about how to manage leg ulcers that keep coming back, and when to treat the varicose veins that may be causing them.

Claim: The current high-certainty evidence shows that ulcer recurrence is the same whether you have combined vein treatment (endovenous ablation) plus compression, or compression alone with or without later vein treatment.

What this means for you:
- The best current evidence shows that adding vein treatment early (combined ablation and compression) does not change your chance of the ulcer coming back.
- Keep wearing your compression therapy. It remains the main treatment while we talk through your options.
- When to treat your veins, early or later, is a choice we can make together. We will weigh your preferences, the risks of the procedure, and the cost.
- The evidence so far comes from only two studies, so we will read both full studies before we finalize the plan.
- We will check your ulcer risk and your treatment choice again at your follow-up visits.

[source: pmid:32965493; pmid:32928070]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your care team is looking at two options for your cancer treatment: chemoradiotherapy (chemotherapy with radiation) alone, or chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery to remove the food pipe (esophagectomy).

Claim: In the short term, quality of life is lower with chemoradiotherapy plus surgery than with chemoradiotherapy alone, and the evidence for this is high-certainty.

What this means for you:
- Adding surgery makes daily life harder for a while after treatment. This is a well-established effect in the research.
- Your team will weigh that short-term burden against the possible benefits of surgery for your cancer. The decision is best made together with your oncology team.
- Please tell us what matters most to you, such as how you function day to day, your symptoms, or your overall goals for treatment. Your priorities will help shape the choice.
- We will plan follow-up to check on your quality of life and symptoms after treatment, whichever approach you choose.

Please bring any questions to your next appointment.

[source: pmid:16524973]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Your care team looked at whether taking a biologic medicine on its own might change your chance of getting cancer, compared with not taking it (placebo). The studies so far suggest that biologic medicines may affect cancer risk, but the evidence is of low certainty, meaning we are not sure how big or real any difference is.

Claim: Biologic medicines alone may change cancer risk compared with placebo, but the evidence is of low certainty.

What this means for you:
- Your treatment will not be changed based on cancer risk from this evidence alone, because we are not confident about the possible difference.
- We will look at your own cancer risk factors, such as family history, smoking, and other personal factors.
- Please keep up with routine cancer screening as you normally would.
- We will revisit this question when better studies comparing the treatments are available.

If you have questions or notice anything new, please contact your care team.

[source: pmid:16162882; pmid:12115176; pmid:24972708]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Your clinician looked at the research on oxytocin and anaemia (low red blood cells) in mothers. The research is not clear. Oxytocin may make maternal anaemia higher, lower, or about the same compared with not using it. The studies are of low certainty, so we cannot say which is true.

Your care will not change because of this result. Your clinician will talk through this with you and will check other sources on anaemia in mothers. If you have questions or notice new symptoms, such as tiredness that is getting worse, dizziness, or shortness of breath, tell your care team.

Claim: Maternal anaemia could be higher, lower, or the same with oxytocin compared with no intervention. The evidence is of low certainty.
[source: pmid:24130463]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: This note is about a possible treatment choice. Endovascular thrombectomy is a procedure that removes a blood clot using a thin tube passed through the blood vessels. "Control" means not having the procedure and getting the usual care instead.

Claim: At 90 days, the risk of death may be the same when comparing endovascular thrombectomy to control (low-certainty evidence).

Your care team plans to talk with you about the chance of death at 90 days when weighing this procedure against control. The research suggests death risk may be no different between the two, but the evidence is low certainty, so this is not settled. Please ask your care team any questions you have about this.

[source: pmid:29129157; pmid:29364767]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your doctor is thinking about whether taking an aromatase inhibitor could help lower your chance of getting breast cancer. This is because you are past menopause and your risk of breast cancer is higher than average.

What we know: compared with a dummy pill (placebo), aromatase inhibitors may lower the overall risk of breast cancer. The evidence for this is low-certainty, so the benefit is uncertain.

This note only covers the possible effect on breast cancer risk. It does not cover other benefits or side effects of these medicines. Those need to be looked at separately before you decide anything.

Please talk with your doctor about whether this option is right for you, and ask about any other effects you should know about.

Claim: Compared with placebo, aromatase inhibitors may lower the overall risk of breast cancer (low-certainty evidence).
[source: pmid:21639806; pmid:24333009]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: Vision screening with free spectacles may make little or no difference to schoolwork compared with vision screening plus spectacles by prescription only. The evidence on this is very uncertain, so we do not know for sure.

Here is what we suggest:

- We will check that your child's vision has been tested and whether glasses are needed.
- If free glasses are available, we can offer them. However, the research does not clearly show that they help school results more than prescription glasses.
- If free glasses are not available, we will continue with prescription glasses and the usual care steps.
- We will keep track of school progress over time, so we can see whether anything changes.
- The main research was done in one large study in China. Things may be different where you live.

[source: pmid:25249453]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: Compared with supportive care, CPAP given early to prevent breathing problems or very early in life makes no difference to the risk of death (high-certainty evidence).

What this means: In the studies that looked at this, babies who received early CPAP and babies who received supportive care had about the same chance of dying. The studies included very low birth weight and preterm babies, including babies treated in the delivery room. Your care team will check whether your situation matches these studies. This is one piece of information. Your doctors will also look at your health right now and use their own judgment to decide between CPAP and supportive care with you.

[source: pmid:22402568; pmid:24554040; pmid:3102211]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: This note explains, in plain words, how your care team is thinking about the way CPR breaths are given.

Claim: Continuous chest compressions with breaths given at separate times, without pausing, may lead to lower survival to hospital discharge than pausing compressions to give breaths, but the evidence for this is very uncertain.

Your team will:
- Check your current resuscitation plan and local guidance on when to give breaths.
- Look for other or newer research, because this conclusion comes from one study.
- Go over this evidence and how certain it is with the resuscitation team.
- Record the evidence and how certain it is in your chart and handoff notes.

[source: pmid:26550795]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Based on the evidence we reviewed, changes to your home, such as screens, window and door fixes, or other housing changes, probably make little or no difference to how often people get clinical malaria, compared with not making any changes. The evidence for this is of moderate certainty.

We would like to talk with you about your housing situation. Changing your home may be one thing you can do to lower your chance of contact with malaria mosquitoes, but it probably will not by itself make much difference to whether you get malaria.

Please keep using the malaria prevention steps that are proven to work:
- Sleep under a bed net every night.
- If you have a fever, get tested for malaria quickly and start treatment straight away if the test is positive.

Please contact your clinic if you have a fever, chills, or feel unwell, especially if you have recently been in an area where malaria is common.

Claim: Housing modifications probably make little or no difference to clinical malaria incidence compared with no modifications; the evidence is of moderate certainty.

[source: pmid:29452110; pmid:33838737; pmid:33640067]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

We do not yet know whether computer-based brain training (computerised cognitive training) that lasts at least 12 weeks is safe or unsafe. The research we have looked at found only weak evidence about side effects. That evidence could show more side effects, fewer side effects, or about the same amount compared with not doing the training. Because of this, please do not assume the training is either safe or risky based on this information.

Claim: The risk of adverse effects could be higher, lower, or the same with computerised cognitive training of at least 12 weeks compared with no intervention. The evidence is of low certainty.

Your care will continue as usual. If computer-based training is being considered for you, your clinician will talk with you about how uncertain this evidence is.

[source: pmid:23531885; pmid:25511081; pmid:20418350]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

We do not know yet whether adding argon laser peripheral iridoplasty (LPIp) to peripheral iridotomy changes your eye pressure (IOP) compared with peripheral iridotomy alone. The research on this is very uncertain, and the quality of the evidence is very low, so this question is still open.

Claim: The evidence is very uncertain about whether mean IOP is the same with argon LPIp added to peripheral iridotomy as with peripheral iridotomy alone; the certainty of this evidence is very low.

[source: pmid:21860572; pmid:20472226]

Because of this uncertainty, your treating ophthalmologist will go over the choice with you. Whichever approach is used, you will still have your usual eye pressure checks after the procedure.

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Your doctor suggests trying computer-based brain training, called computerised cognitive training (CCT), for at least 12 weeks to help with memory. Keep your expectations realistic. Your doctor will review with you at your next visit how much it has helped.

Claim: Memory for past events is higher at the end of at least 12 weeks of computer-based training than with no training, and high-certainty evidence from one study shows this benefit.
[source: pmid:20418350]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Based on the studies comparing belimumab with a placebo (dummy treatment), the evidence about whether belimumab changes your risk of one or more serious infections is very uncertain. The studies so far do not show a clear difference in risk between belimumab and placebo, but the evidence is of very low quality, so we cannot be confident about this finding.

Claim: Compared with placebo, belimumab may not be associated with a higher or lower risk of one or more serious infections, but the evidence is very uncertain (very-low-certainty evidence).

[source: pmid:19714604; pmid:28118533; pmid:22127708; pmid:21296403]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU, here is what your care team has planned for your ovarian cyst.

There are two ways to manage it: draining the cyst with a needle (aspiration) or watching it over time without draining it (conservative management). The research we have shows that these two approaches give the same chance of a clinical pregnancy. Draining the cyst is not expected to improve your chances of becoming pregnant.

So the choice between them should depend on the cyst's features, your symptoms, and what you prefer. Before your visit, the team will review both studies that the plan is based on. We will check the cyst again if it changes or if new research comes out.

Claim: There is no difference in clinical pregnancy rate between ovarian cyst aspiration and conservative management (high-certainty evidence).

[source: pmid:2120087; pmid:16253965]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Here is what the study evidence says about alpha-lipoic acid for nerve pain or tingling in the feet and hands. We are not sure yet whether it helps or hurts compared with a dummy pill (placebo) after six months. The information we have is limited.

Claim: The evidence is very uncertain about whether alpha-lipoic acid has no difference from placebo on TSS neuropathy symptoms at six months, and comes from one trial.

What this means for you:
- The one study that looked at this (a 7-month trial called ALADIN III) found no clear difference in your symptom score, but the evidence is very weak, so this result should not be treated as a firm answer.
- Whether alpha-lipoic acid makes your symptoms better or worse compared with placebo is still very uncertain.
- Your clinician will weigh this uncertain result together with your own symptoms, your preferences, and other treatment options you could consider.
- This advice may change as more research becomes available, so your care plan may be reviewed over time.

Please talk with your clinician before starting, stopping, or changing any treatment.

[source: pmid:10480774]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: The evidence is very uncertain about whether smart technology for self-management increases activity levels up to 6 months compared with face-to-face, digital, or written support (very low-certainty evidence).
[source: pmid:25811395; pmid:27502583]
[AI-generated]

Here is what this means for you. Researchers are not sure whether using a smart device to manage your own health makes you more active over the next 6 months. Compared with seeing someone in person, using a computer or app, or getting written advice, the results are unclear. The studies that looked at this were both about people with COPD, and they used a pedometer (a device that counts steps) with an internet walking program.

Your care team may suggest the following:

- Talk with them about whether a pedometer or similar step-counting device with an online walking program would fit your goals and your daily routine.
- Agree on a step goal that feels realistic for you, and check your progress together at regular times.
- Keep your current face-to-face or written support in place. The device is not known to replace it.
- Let your team know how your activity, symptoms, and quality of life are going over time. If you are not improving, or if the program is hard to keep up with, the plan can be changed.
- Keep in mind that these studies were done in people with COPD, so the results may apply less directly if you have a different condition.

Please ask your clinician if you have questions about any of this.

FOR YOU

Claim: The evidence is very uncertain about whether treatment-related death is higher when chemoradiotherapy is followed by surgery (esophagectomy) than when chemoradiotherapy is used alone. The quality of this evidence is very low, so this finding should be given very little weight.

What this means for you:
- Nobody can say with confidence whether adding surgery raises the chance of dying from treatment. The studies that looked at this question do not give a clear answer.
- Your care team will check how fit you are for surgery. This includes your heart and lung function, your nutrition, and how well you are able to carry on with daily activities. These things affect how safe surgery would be for you.
- Your team will talk with you about the possible benefits of surgery, such as better control of the cancer in the area, and weigh them against the uncertain extra risk. This will be a decision you make together with your doctors.
- Chemoradiotherapy alone is a reasonable option. It may be the better choice if surgery carries a high risk for you, or if you would prefer to avoid an operation. Your team will explain their reasoning.
- Treatment guidelines and newer studies are checked regularly, and this advice is based on only two studies. Please ask your team about the latest information.

Please bring any questions to your next appointment with your surgical and oncology team.

[source: pmid:17401004; pmid:15800321]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: Overall survival may be higher, lower, or the same with percutaneous ethanol injection (PEI) compared with no treatment. The evidence is of low certainty, so we cannot say which is likely.

What this means:
- The studies we found do not compare PEI directly with no treatment. They compare PEI with other treatments, so they give only indirect clues.
- Because the evidence is weak, it is not a good basis for choosing treatment by expected survival alone.
- Your care team can talk with you about the treatments that were compared with PEI in these studies: surgical removal of the tumor, radiofrequency ablation (heat treatment), and acetic acid injection.
- The choice depends on your tumor's size, how well your liver works, and your overall health. Your doctors can review current liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma) guidelines and may seek a liver or cancer specialist's opinion to help decide.

[source: pmid:9425919; pmid:16009687; pmid:15973099]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Your baby's care team will keep following the unit's usual feeding plan. They will decide case by case, using their clinical judgement, whether to give back or throw away any milk left in your baby's stomach.

Claim: For premature babies, we are very unsure whether giving back stomach milk instead of throwing it away changes how long it takes to reach full feeds. This is based on very low-certainty evidence from a single trial.

[source: pmid:25552280]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU
Your care team is thinking about a urine test called LAM, which can help check for tuberculosis (TB) in people with HIV who are in hospital. It is a quick test done at the bedside. It would be used along with the usual TB tests, not in place of them. Your team will look at the result together with everything else about your health.

Claim: Using the urine LAM test may be linked to fewer deaths by eight weeks than routine TB testing alone, but the evidence for this is very uncertain.

The studies behind this come from two trials, and they may not match every hospital or every patient. Your team will keep checking how you are doing.

[source: pmid:30032978; pmid:26970721]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your clinician is looking at whether computerised cognitive training (CCT) might help your overall thinking ability. Here is what we know so far.

Claim: Global cognitive function may differ after at least 12 weeks of computerised cognitive training compared with no intervention; the evidence is of low certainty.

What this means for you:
- The studies found a possible effect of CCT on overall thinking ability, but the evidence is weak, so we cannot be sure.
- If you want to try CCT, think of it as an option, not a proven benefit.
- Your cognitive function will continue to be checked as usual, and your care plan will be reviewed if new evidence becomes available.
- The clinician can go through three studies with you. They looked at combined cognitive and physical training, strength and balance training with CCT, and complex mental and physical activity in older women. These can show you what was tested.

Please ask your clinician any questions you have.

[source: pmid:23531885; pmid:25511081; pmid:20418350]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Here is a short summary of what the research found about giving carbohydrate supplements to babies to lower the risk of necrotising enterocolitis (NEC), a serious bowel condition that can affect premature babies.

Claim: Based on moderate-certainty evidence, there is probably no difference in NEC risk between giving carbohydrate supplements and not giving them. The true effect is probably close to this estimate, although a meaningful effect in either direction remains possible.

What this means: One randomised trial looked at this question. It found that carbohydrate supplements did not clearly change the chance of NEC. Because the evidence comes from a single study, it should not by itself change how babies are fed. Your baby's care team will look at local NEC prevention guidance and your baby's individual needs, such as gestational age, how well they tolerate feeds, and other risk factors, before deciding whether supplements are right for them. If you have questions, please ask your care team.

[source: pmid:25538834]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your care team looked at the best information available about video calls. It suggests that video calls probably make little or no difference to how well you feel you can do your physical activities and roles, compared with your usual care. The evidence for this is moderate in certainty, which means it is a reasonable guide but not a final answer.

The main study behind this is a smartphone-based video call program for older nursing home residents. It looked at depression, loneliness, and quality of life, not specifically physical roles, so it may not fully match your situation.

What happens next:
- Your care team will talk with you about your own physical function and what matters most to you.
- Your usual care stays as the baseline.
- Video calls are an option you can choose if you want them.
- If you try them, you and your team can track how your physical-role quality of life changes over time, so you can see what works for you.

Claim: For this question, video calls probably make little or no difference to physical-role quality of life compared with usual care, with moderate-certainty evidence.

[source: pmid:31992217]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your care team is looking at whether exercise can help your balance. The studies they reviewed mostly looked at men on hormone-blocking treatment for prostate cancer and at breast cancer survivors with bone loss. The results are very uncertain. We do not yet know for sure whether exercise helps your balance more than your usual care.

Claim: The evidence is very uncertain about whether balance on the backward walk test is higher with exercise than with usual care; the certainty of the evidence is very low.

Here is what your team plans to do:
- They may suggest a program that combines strength exercises and aerobic exercise, along with your usual care.
- They will record a starting backward walk test, so your progress can be compared over time.
- They will check how your balance is doing and how well you tolerate the program at your next visit, then decide whether to continue.
- Because the studies did not look at people exactly like you, your team will think carefully about how well the results fit your situation.

Please tell your care team if you have any dizziness, pain, or falls during exercise.

[source: pmid:19949016; pmid:19335674]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Your doctor is looking at two treatments for the build-up of fluid in your belly (ascites) caused by cirrhosis. One is a procedure called TIPS. The other is draining the fluid (paracentesis) with an albumin infusion.

Research we are highly confident in shows that the two treatments do not differ in how many people die from any cause.

Your doctor will talk this through with you and with the liver specialists (hepatology) before choosing. The choice will depend on your overall health and what matters to you. The plan will be looked at again as new research becomes available.

Claim: TIPS and conventional treatment have the same effect on all-cause mortality, and the certainty of the evidence is high.

[source: pmid:12454841; pmid:10841872]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your doctor has looked at the evidence on two types of botulinum toxin used for neck muscle problems (cervical dystonia). Botulinum toxin type A (BtA) is less likely than type B (BtB) to cause a sore throat or dry mouth as a side effect. The studies behind this are fairly strong.

Claim: Compared with BtB, BtA is less likely to cause a sore throat or dry mouth (high-certainty evidence).

What this means for you:
- Before choosing a type, your doctor will ask about any trouble swallowing, dry mouth, or throat problems you already have.
- If BtA is used, a sore throat or dry mouth is less likely than with BtB, but it can still happen.
- If BtB is considered, your doctor will talk with you about these side effects being more common, and will watch for them after the injection.
- At follow-up, tell your doctor about any changes in your throat or mouth, so they can be written down and tracked.

[source: pmid:16275831; pmid:18098274]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Here is what this means for your care.

Claim: Oxytocin may change the rate of breastfeeding compared with no intervention, although the direction of any effect remains unclear. The certainty of the evidence is low.

Your care team will not change feeding decisions based on this evidence. Whether you receive oxytocin depends mainly on why it is being used, such as to help prevent heavy bleeding after birth, and not on its expected effect on breastfeeding. You will keep the usual breastfeeding support and monitoring that every new parent receives. If breastfeeding outcomes matter for a decision about your care, ask your clinician, because the study cited here reports on bleeding after birth, not on breastfeeding itself.

[source: pmid:24130463]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: Based on the current research, it is not yet clear whether computerised cognitive training for 12 weeks or longer changes your daily living abilities (such as dressing, cooking, or managing money). The evidence is of low certainty, so it could help, make no difference, or make things somewhat worse. Because of this, we should not use this evidence alone to decide on training for your daily function.

What this means for you:

- We cannot promise that brain training will improve how you manage everyday tasks.
- We will check how you are doing with everyday activities now, using a standard scale, and again at follow-up, so we can see any change clearly.
- If you would like to try cognitive training, it can be a choice for your thinking skills or your overall wellbeing. We will review your everyday function at set times while you do it.
- We will look at this question again when studies that measure everyday activities as a main outcome become available.

Please bring any questions to your next appointment.

[source: pmid:27698558; pmid:29261218; pmid:21615936; pmid:26417460; pmid:21311196; pmid:23531885]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Here is a short plan about dressings for your open wound.

Claim: For your wound, the research probably gives a fairly good idea of how much a special suction dressing (called NPWT, set at 75 mmHg) may lower the chance of infection compared with standard care. The evidence is moderate in strength.

Your care team will choose between the suction dressing and standard care. They will think about the shape and depth of your wound, whether it is dirty or contaminated, your own health, and local hospital rules.

- If you get the suction dressing, the team will check your wound for signs of infection at each routine visit and write down what they find.
- If you get standard care, you will get the same checks and the same wound care plan.
- The plan may change if new research comes out.
- The main study behind this advice was one trial of this dressing for serious dog bites on arms and legs. Your wound is a different kind of injury, so the results may not apply to you directly.

Please ask your care team if you have questions about which option is right for you.

[source: pmid:26964825]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Whether adding the MVA85A vaccine to the BCG vaccine, compared with BCG alone, changes your risk of getting tuberculosis that is confirmed by a lab test is very uncertain. The evidence for this is of very low certainty. This means there may be no difference, but we cannot be sure.

The main study behind this comes from healthy adults who have HIV-1. So its results may apply most directly to people in a similar situation.

A second study in this set looks at tooth decay on the chewing surfaces of teeth. It does not look at MVA85A or tuberculosis, so it is not used for this decision.

Before making a decision, your clinician will check the full study reports and current national guidance. The plan will be reviewed if new evidence appears.

Claim: There may be no difference in the risk of microbiologically confirmed tuberculosis between MVA85A added to BCG and BCG alone, but the evidence is very uncertain (very-low-certainty evidence).

[source: pmid:25726088; pmid:23391465]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: Video calls probably make little or no difference to depression at 1 year compared with usual care. The certainty of the evidence is moderate.

Your care team is looking at research on video calls and depression. Here is what that research suggests, in plain words:

- Video calls probably do not change depression much over one year, compared with the usual care people get. The evidence is fairly good, but not certain.
- This means your care team will not change your treatment based on this research alone.
- Your team will keep checking your mood over time with a standard questionnaire, both now and at follow-up visits.
- Your team would like to know your wishes about video calls, and whether you can access them easily. If you use video calls, tracking your mood and how much contact you have with others can help.
- The research was a single study of older adults living in nursing homes, in a video call program lasting at least 3 months. It may not match your situation.
- Your team will look at this question again if better research becomes available.

[source: pmid:22086660]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: The evidence is very uncertain about whether dihydrocodeine (DHC) and buprenorphine lead to similar rates of detoxification at six-month follow-up. Because of this, the research gives very little guidance on which one is better for this purpose.

Here is what this means for you:

- The studies do not show clearly whether the two medicines work about the same for stopping opioid use by six months.
- Your doctor will not choose between them based on this comparison alone. Other things matter too, such as side effects, how well each medicine is tolerated, what is available, how you responded to treatment before, and what you prefer.
- You will have follow-up appointments so your doctor can check how you are doing and change the plan if needed.
- If you want more detail, your doctor can look at the original studies with you.

If you have questions about your treatment, please ask your doctor or care team.

[source: pmid:19196468; pmid:17210079]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Your care team may suggest a program called targeted, comprehensive occupational therapy, given alongside your usual care. Its aim is to help you keep working. Your team will talk with you about whether it fits your situation.

Claim: Intermediate-term work functioning is higher with non-pharmacological job loss prevention interventions than with usual care, and the evidence establishes this benefit with high certainty.

In plain words: this claim is based on one study, in people with rheumatoid arthritis. In that study, people who received this occupational therapy had better daily functioning and work outcomes. Your team will first check whether you have a condition similar to that study group. They will also measure your work functioning at the start and again at a later follow-up.

[source: pmid:19877106]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

We are talking about your caffeine choices, and what the research says about them. Right now the evidence is very uncertain.

Claim: Based on very low-certainty evidence from one trial, it is very uncertain whether birth weight differs between caffeinated and decaffeinated instant coffee. [source: pmid:17259189]

The studies behind this come from one randomised trial that looked at cutting down caffeine intake. That trial was small and the evidence is of very low certainty, so we cannot say with confidence whether caffeinated or decaffeinated instant coffee makes a difference to birth weight.

Because of this, let's look at your overall caffeine intake from all sources, not only instant coffee. This includes tea, cola, chocolate, and energy drinks. Once we have the full picture, we can agree on a plan together that works for you.

We will also check back on this question if new evidence becomes available.

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Here is what the research says about adding indoor spraying to bed nets for malaria.

Claim: Adding pyrethroid-like indoor residual spraying (IRS) to insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) may not change how many people have malaria parasites compared with using nets alone, but the evidence is very uncertain.

What this means for you:
- Keep using your insecticide-treated net every night. Nets are the standard protection.
